item.title: The Surprising Reality of Living Offline
item.description:
It’s a dream a lot of us have: to finally say “enough!”, and turn off the internet inside our homes, returning us to a lifestyle that requires more presence, introspection, and connection. But is this even possible? And what would it really be like? In this episode, Cal seeks answers to these questions by talking to Chris Moody, a journalism professor at Appalachian State, who lives with his wife and young son in a cabin with no internet, television, or cellular signal.
More from Cal
Download Cal’s FREE guide to cultivating a deeper life: calnewport.com/ideas Learn more about Cal’s books: calnewport.com/books Listen to Cal’s podcast: thedeeplife.com/listen

Should I turn off the internet?

Have you ever had one of those days where you're so fed up from the constant connectivity and the distraction that you wish you could just turn back the clock to the 1990s? I mean, I'm talking about a time where work couldn't easily follow you home. Like, if your boss wanted you after hours, he would have to call you on a landline. A time where you could build a delightful evening out of whatever random video you're able to pick up at the rental store. Well, not long ago, I met someone who is doing exactly this. His name is

Chris Moody. He teaches journalism at Appalachian State in Boone, North Carolina, which is a a small scenic town that's perched right off of the Blue Ridge Parkway. Now, Chris lives along with his wife and his young son in a cabin that's located about 15 minutes outside of town that receives no cell reception and has no internet. Their only connection to the outside world is a landline phone. Now, this disconnection is on purpose. Chris and his wife used to live a frenetic life in

New York City, where Chris was a senior correspondent for CNN politics, but after the pandemic hit, they decided to live more intentionally. Now, Chris's situation raises some fascinating questions. What's it actually like to live in 1990s mode? and what lessons can the rest of us learn from his experience? Well, it's Monday, which means it's time for an advice episode of this show, which is the perfect opportunity to seek some answers. So, here's what I did. I called up Chris because I want to find out more about what led him to that

cabin in Boone. What is the actual reality of his current life? I have a bunch of questions about some like in the weeds details about how does he do this and how does he do that? Um, and most importantly, what lessons can we extract for the rest of us who might also be tempted to try something extreme in the quest for a deeper life? Now, look, I love this conversation. You'll hear it in my voice. I I was expecting to come away with mixed emotions, like that was cool, but that seems like it was pretty hard. Um, but to be honest, it was almost entirely inspiring. I I think Chris's brand of hybrid simplicity

really is pretty compelling, especially when he discusses the impact of this way of living on his young son. Let me give you a spoiler from later in the interview. He tells me about uh recently taking his three-year-old son to a modern dance performance. They were sitting in the front row. And he said his three-year-old son, who has only grown up around 1990s tech, none of these like screens and iPads and Bluey or whatever, was able to sit and give full focus to this modern dance performance while the boomers around them couldn't help but fidget and look

at their phones before the performance ended. All right. All right. So, anyways, look, if you've um if you've ever felt like taking an extreme step towards intentional living, but are maybe worried about the reality or looking for some inspiration to make changes, you have to listen to this episode. Uh I think you're going to love it. As always, I'm Cal Newport and this is Deep Questions, the show for people seeking depth in a distracted world. Well, Chris, I'm glad we finally found

this opportunity to get you on the show.

Interview with Chris Moody

I feel like I talk about you to people all the time, so now we can actually uh spread your story more widely. Um, I wanted to start if you could just set the stage about where you currently live and what that lifestyle is like and then we'll go back and kind of build up the story to how you got there. Well, thanks so much for having me on the show, Cal. It's great to be here. Uh, I live in southern Appalachia in Boone, North Carolina, uh, with my wife and my son. He, uh, is three years old now. And for the past 3 years, we've been living in a

log cabin without internet access or cell phone service. We're kind of deep in the hauler, so the cell phone towers don't really get to us. And, uh, 3 years ago, we went to the cable company and had our Wi-Fi turned off and had a landline plugged in. Um we did that for many reasons that you and I will discuss today. But um we realized that the life of permanent constant digital connection was not serving us, was not serving our family life. And um I found it personally to be so powerful and

intoxicating that the only thing we decided we could do was to cut it off inside our home and live a life together um in our home without digital connection. Um we certainly engage with the internet outside of the home, but when we're at home, it is our sanctuary, our Sabbath space, and we did that for for many many reasons. Um we started doing it when my son was just a couple of months old. So, an infant in the house. And anyone who has children knows what a household like that is is like. And I found myself, especially

[clears throat] after our son was born, just getting deeper and deeper into screen time. Um, as maybe a lot of people can relate. I think my my screen time app at that time had said maybe four, six, maybe even sometimes eight hours a day just looking at the phone. Um, when you have a newborn in the house, there's a lot of sitting around together, waiting, um, just being together. And I would pull out the phone and just scroll, scroll, scroll. It got worse and worse and worse. And my wife told me that when you pull out your phone, it's as though you disappear. And I started to think, is this what life is

going to be like for the rest of our lives? Cuz it's pretty mediocre. I'm not really enjoying this. And one day I said to my wife, I I I I I think we need to do something different. And she said, "Sounds like we should get rid of the internet." I said, 'When? She said,"Right now." It was something we thought we'd do for a couple of months, maybe for a summer. That was 3 years ago, and we have not gone back. And um it's the greatest decision I've ever made. >> I have a long list of questions about the the reality of your internet free life, but let's now let's back up the tape to get to this point. So, where I'm

going to start is how did you end up in Boone, right? Um, so where were you before that? Because I I get the feeling the move there, you were already thinking in terms of >> being intentional about your life. So, so back up the tape to before you moved to the Hollers of North Carolina and how that decision emerged. Well, I was a senior correspondent for CNN politics covering presidential campaigns, Congress, um, and living in Washington DC and later New York City. And as you might imagine, a life of a political

journalist is very connected. I was working constantly. Work was my life. It was my religion. It was my um, it was everything at that time. And I would be connected in the middle of the night. I would wake up and check stories to make sure they were okay. I would check social media. Uh if I told you at that time that I had a hobby, I would have been lying. Work was everything to me. Um and and so I always dreamed of a time like maybe someday I could live and be disconnected or or something like that. And my wife had been talking about doing

this in in different ways, but it just was impossible as a political correspondent in DC and in New York. Um [clears throat] and um and but we would play around with this at times. We would um in our apartment in New York City where of course you know you can't get away from cell service or anything like that um we would put our our phones in baskets by the door um between like and p.m. And we would call that cabining. Kind of pretending that we were off the grid for just 2 hours. And it felt so rebellious to just be alone together without any chance of anyone

reaching us even just for a couple of hours. Uh and we realized the the freedom of time. It it hearken back uh listeners might have experienced this. You go on vacation in the 1990s or something like that to a cabin or a lakehouse and time sort of expands. The there's no phone, there's no internet, there's I mean back then certainly and you were just alone with your family playing back gammon taking long walks having those deep conversations. Um that cabin life that we cherish on those long summer days. Uh over time when I would meet with my family um those cabin days

started to dwindle down. U first it was flip phone games and then it was laptops out in the common area and until finally it was smartphones and all that kind of deep time we had together was was slowly eroding. Um and fast forward to the 201s, my wife and I really wanted to kind of take back what it felt to be in a cabin in our apartment in Manhattan in New York City. Um and so we had these kind of small little um rebellions, things like that. It just it it felt uh like we were getting away with

something. Um then in 2018, uh there was a reshuffleling at the the network where I worked and um I was laid off and we had an opportunity at last to kind of give up that digital connection. So, we actually gave away most of our possessions and we built a solar powered tiny house into the back of a used cargo van. And my wife and I lived for 2 years um traveling the country in a cargo van uh living in national forests, national parks um mostly off the grid. um largely in search of other people that were

dissatisfied with modern life and finding alternatives and new ways to opt out of modern um kind of distraction and opt into new ways of of living. And um and then we took that um and then actually moved back to New York City right before COVID started. And we had we had never uh installed the internet into our apartment, our new apartment in New York. So, we were living internet free in an apartment in New York City and then COVID happened and everything went online and CO kind of moved us out of New York City again and um we ended

up in Boone, North Carolina where I teach journalism at Appalachin State University. Um, and that presented itself this wonderful opportunity. Here was a place where we live that does not have cell service because it's rural and we can turn off the internet um and have that log cabin experience that we always wanted to have. And now we're doing it with a child in the home and and the challenges that come with that. Um, being able to keep the culture at bay and then allow it into our home um on our own terms and not on its terms. And

that's really what motivates us. >> Hey, let's take a quick break to hear from some of the sponsors that make the show possible. Have you ever had that experience where you put something off again and again and then when you finally get around to doing it, you kick yourself for having waited so long? I mean, I felt that way about this podcast. People kept telling me, "You need your own show." And I agreed, but I didn't want to bother. And then once I finally did start it, I was like, "Oh man, should have done this a while ago." Well, I don't want you to feel this way about that business idea that you have been sitting on. This is why you need Shopify because it makes

getting started selling things easy, providing everything you need to turn your idea into action. For example, all Shopify storefronts are integrated with Shopify checkout, which helps your customers finish their purchases, and when they come back, all of their information is already saved. This not only converts more customers, but gives you more time to focus on what really matters, improving your products and growing your business. If we ever start selling things here at the show, we will for sure use Shopify. I'm always happy when I come across a Shopify powered store as I know my purchasing experience

will be seamless and easy. So, if you've been sitting on an idea for a business, Shopify can make it easy to get started. With Shopify, nothing stands between your idea and a real business. So, go make one. If you're starting, if you're ready to stop putting off your business and start hearing, then you're ready for Shopify. Start your free trial at shopify.com/deep today. You heard that right. Start your free trial today at shopify.com/deep. That's shopify.com/deep.

I also want to talk about our friends at Piperive. Here's a stat that genuinely shocked me. Sales teams spend about 50% of their time on admin work instead of selling, building relationships, or closing deals. This pseudo productivity is devastating to the bottom line. Fortunately, this is where today's sponsor, Pipe Drive, comes in. Here's what I love about Pipe Drive. It is a fantastic sales CRM system that's built with small and medium-sized businesses in mind. It's built from the ground up to strip away repetitive work. Smart automations can handle shallow tasks like reminders, deal updates, and

activity logging. And you can customize all of this automation to fit your unique sales process. Not sure where there's room for improvement? Use their AI features to analyze your pipeline and surface what needs attention. If your business sells things, you need Pipe Drive. It's time to switch to a CRM built by salespeople for salespeople and join the over 100,000 companies already using Piperive. My link gets you an exclusive 30 days free instead of the usual 14-day trial. No credit card or payment needed. Just head to

piperive.com/deep to get started. That's piperive.com/deep and you can be up and running in minutes. All right, let's get back to the show. Well, [laughter] first of all, disclaimer for the audience who is watching who's wondering where is Chris talking from. That is not his cabin. There is no internet there. He's actually on vacation. And this is a would you say a friend's barn. Is that how you described it? >> Okay. >> Yes. But has Wi-Fi, thank goodness. Yeah. >> I have to back you up though about this cargo van situation. Like, okay, let let's go there. First of all, when you say cargo van, are we talking about one

of those Sprinter vans or are we talking about one of those like white, you know, vans that the painters drive around? >> It's a white Ram ProMaster, like a something that an electrical company or a painter would would have. Um, and [clears throat] it was nondescript because our plan was to live as long as we could um without paying rent. uh we were paying off about a lot of student loans, let's just say in the six figures of student loans. Um and we were just trying to live rent free so we could pay off our our student loans. And um we just lived in places that didn't have access to the internet. We learned the joy of of living together

without those distractions as a couple. Um at this time we did not have a child. um and and getting to know one another kind of on those terms and and realizing what an abundant rich life that we had together um without constant distractions in our lives that we had when we lived in New York and in Washington. >> Where were some of the places Where were some of the places you went? >> Well, we did 50,000 miles um we would kind of go back and forth following the weather. We didn't have heat or air conditioning in the back cabin of the of the van. So, we would follow, you know, when it got hot, we went up, when it got

cold, we went down, you know. Um, and that that included national forests out in the west. Uh, you know, for for anyone interested in this, you can camp for free all over the United States of America and Canada and Mexico if you want to, you know, um, and and so you don't always have to like pay for a campsite. And we built systems into our van that allowed us to be off-rid um, for long periods of time in in many ways. And uh it uh it transformed the way we approach a more normal life today with a child, with a job, with a house um and and not just um traveling around

in a van. >> Like what let's let's say like I'm just fascinated by this. So So let's say it's like a day where you're not driving, you're parked at a state park somewhere, you know, out west. What would you do during that day? >> I wake up. Yes. Wake up. We have enough solar power from the sun to boil one pot of water for our coffee. We sit and read for 3 hours in the morning, go out into the woods, collect um collect wood for a fire, uh build a fire, have breakfast, um maybe take a hike, uh do some

writing, you know, I maybe I travel into town, get on Wi-Fi, uh send pitches to editors. I'm a writer. Um you know, write magazine stories and things like that. um then go back into the woods and and write and cook and read. It was really was a really ideal kind of kind of situation. Um and then pack up the van and move on to the next place, however long we were staying somewhere. But it involved a lot of reading, a lot of writing, a lot of time together really understanding how we wanted to live. we were um you know um on the brink of of wanting to start a family

and have children and just it was really a a blessing to be able to think deeply about the kinds of Americans, the kinds of people we wanted to be. I'll tell you it really feels like living the standard way where you just go with the flow is not leading people to a happy place. Um, I think you need to be intentional and follow your north star and know what that is. But you have to give yourself the time to understand what you think about things. And I feel like with so many distractions coming at us, so much content flooding our lives and our even our most private spaces, people don't

really have the time anymore to think what is the good life? What is the life I want to live? And this provided us with that time um to come to those conclusions together. So you were getting you were getting insight because you could introspect. So you're getting insight into what mattered to you and your wife. Um and it the answer was not we want to just live in a van forever. It was more the simplicity of the van gave you the time and space to figure out what you actually cared about. Is that the way you would think about it? >> Yes. We paired everything down to its just most basic forms. We only had a

couple of hundred um of watts of solar. So very limited amounts of power. We had 72 square ft for two people. Um, you know, you can imagine the privacy. You know, you got to be with someone you really trust and know and like, you know, a lot. Um, there's nowhere to escape arguments. You're together all of the time. Not just together, but 5t from each other. You only have a couple pairs of clothes, kind of a capsule wardrobe. Uh, just living very, very simply. There's no room to store anything like that. Um, and that getting those distractions out and just focusing on

the essentials of life. something as simple as what do we eat today? Okay, do we have enough water? We have to collect water. We have to collect wood. Um those kinds of of chores. And I'll tell you um just from a from a family perspective, the time in the van kind of made me realize that I had been a lazy husband because in 72 ft Cal um if one person is lounging and the other person is working, there's no escaping the contrast. So I'd be lying on the bed reading while my wife maybe is cooking dinner and I it was just so obvious the the balance of labor was completely off.

And so we had to do things together and continue till the job was done. There was no, you know, husband kind of escaping to another room and not being found, you know, and it it frankly it made me a much better husband in in realizing the the work that I needed to do to make the the household run or in our case the van the van. Um and then the question was going forward, how do we apply this to a more normal life? And I think we got sidetracked a little bit and uh with the intoxication of modern life when we came back from the woods so to speak. Um but we in our current lifestyle living in a log cabin without

the internet we have really found what we were looking for uh the entire time. >> So what are what are some of the other like insights you had during that experience that you've now carried through to the life you created? Now I'm curious and like what type of epiphies one might have in those situations. U there were so many um certainly um communicating with with one another um just as a as a married couple getting you know doing things together um learning that time when it's not distracted and punctuated by those distraction can expand and feels almost

luxurious to have time together where there aren't things that you're seeking for just constant consumption constant entertainment. Living with very little will make you think a lot about kind of how much you consume, how much you things you own, how much water you use, um those kinds of things, how much power you use. We had to get by on very very little power and just as much water as we could carry. Um and so it just makes you hyper aware of all of those all of those things. Um but but also just the contrast of going back into society,

maybe having dinner at a restaurant and you know sometimes they have TVs at a sports bar or something and once you've been in the woods for long enough, television and commercials start to look crazy to you. Uh just [clears throat] it just everything is is kind of lower quality in terms of the things that they're advertising don't look enticing anymore. you've had the richness of the woods, the richness of nature, of of true quality time with one another, and you go and you watch an ad for a new Verizon cell phone, you're just like, I don't I don't really want that, you know. Um uh or certainly um coming back

into a city and this was a time in the mid20s when we were making the transition to 100% smartphone adoption for the most part and the streaming wars. And so all of the sudden, the world had shifted while I had been in the woods for a couple of years. And now there are all these things I'd never heard of. Disney Plus, Apple Plus, all those kinds of things during that time. And it it was as though there was just a flood of consumption content being put on people. Uh and it was really overwhelming um to see. Everybody else had kind of gone through it like a

slowly boiled frog and we just jumped into the deep end very quickly. And to to see that contrast um just it it allowed us to know what we want and what we don't want. And sometimes you have to separate yourself from the culture in order to see it clearly. Otherwise, we're really just kind of looking at it as as part of it. You do have to back up a little bit. But you can only do that if you allow yourself the space to do it. >> Now, I imagine being a political like a reporter in a major city. Like there's two big driving forces are hard to escape would be money and fame. Like

you're a reporter in New York City, you're like, I guess I want to be Anderson Cooper. I want to be Jake Tapper or what have you. How did your your thinking about money and fame and notoriety, how did that change when you got some space from it? >> That's a hard one. It really is because it is fun to be on TV. It is fun to have your name published in in major publications and and I still I still do that, you know, um and I get to use those those skills, but in a way you are saying goodbye. I I think it was a real wrestling um in our minds when we decided to leave New York. I didn't want

to go. I I I you know, I grew up, you know, in the suburbs. It was just kind of like a normal town. And to be in New York was everything to me. It was the epitome of all of my life's work dreams. And to leave it um was was very difficult. But Cal, I had made work my identity. I had made it my idol. And that's an unhealthy relationship with work. And and I think leaving that allowed me to have a better relationship

with work, to allow me to do what I want to do, to write what I wish to write and appear, you know, I continue to appear on shows, things like this. Um, and but not have it consume my life in the way. I have no regrets that I was able to do that incredible work, travel around the country, chase Donald Trump around, you know, ask him questions, those kinds of things as a reporter. Um, absolutely loved doing it for that season of life. Um, but uh I never would have been living the way I am. Never would have been raising my son the way that I am. Um, if we hadn't left, uh, his life in Manhattan, if he were living there now,

would be extremely different than it is now in a log cabin where he has access to the woods, the streams, the rivers, the trees, you know, um, it's it's really an abundant life I think we're giving to him. Well, >> so moving forward the the tape a little bit more. So you returned to New York, COVID hits, you're like, "Okay, we're going to leave here." How did you end up where you are right now? So how did Boon enter the the picture once you decided like, "Okay." Yeah. >> Yeah. We got back into the van. Um traveled south just kind of looking for the next steps. This is in the early

days of co things are really dark at that time. Um spent some time in Chattanooga, Tennessee where we have family. um lived there for just a little bit and um then there was an opening for a teaching position at Appalachin State University in journalism and broadcast media um things that I've done for many many years and uh uh I applied and they uh gave me an invitation to come and uh at that time we were just finding out that we had a baby coming on the way and we had been traveling for five six years at that time kind of off and on a very

you know jet setting or van setting kind of life um We had lived all over the country. Um we only had a van with two seats. We didn't have health insurance, you know, uh and the the thought of of uh having a little bit more security when my wife gives birth and we can raise a child was was very enticing. The ability to to teach and also continue writing. And that's how we got to to Boone, which is a lovely small town in a medium-sized small town, I would say, um in northwestern North Carolina, right on the Blue Ridge Parkway. um and uh has a large public university part of the UNC

system and um and we found uh this cabin in the hauler and turned off the internet and that's how we've been living. >> So what's the town like? So it's it's a college town. Um is it like I was just in Asheville recently which I know is in the general sphere. It's like a smaller version of Asheville. Like you have like an old down old historic downtown and you have like standard suburbs I assume. like what's the what's the vibe like in the actual town? >> Much smaller than Asheville, not standard suburbs. People live um either in the town or in the county in the

mountains. Um so there's a pretty hard drop between city life and then mountain life. There are student housing of course around the the town, but not suburbs and the sprawl in any way that you might consider in a place like Asheville or something like that. Um there's about 20,000 people plus the students which is about 20,000. So the city expands and retracts um throughout the year and um it's uh you know it is a college town but it's also a tourist town. It's where people come and a lot of flidians have second homes there. Um and and so you have an interaction that

swings between 20 year olds to 70 year olds, you know, and then the major employers in Boon are the university, the hospital, and um there's a major nonprofit there as well. Um Franklin Graham's Samaritan's Purse is there. So you have a a really um a really neat mix of people. It is a place of very high social trust, which I value very much. When I'm working in coffee shops, I don't even think twice about leaving my laptop on the desk. I don't even ask somebody to look for it, look look after it when I step out um for a moment. It um it it's really it's a place where your kids can run in the woods, where

they can play in the parks, where parents don't necessarily hover over their kids very much. You can always tell when somebody's from out of town because they're kind of following their children around the playground. Um and and so uh you know and it's also a place where people really came together when Hurricane Helen hit very very hard at that time and we really learned who our neighbors were and we found that they were incredible people that look after each other. So it's um it's a pretty splendid uh place there in the in the mountains. Um it you know it's part of the Appalachian. It's the highest um east of the Mississippi highest mountains. Um and so we have ski resorts and it's uh it's an ideal place to live

for sure. >> Yeah. So when you when you were coming out there to take the position, it seems like it would have been a no-brainer, I guess, right? You're like, "Look, we will live not in town, but in the mountains because then we have cabin life, but we can also I can go work at a coffee shop or at my office at campus." So, was that a no-brainer when you got there? Like, yeah, this is great. Let's find something like a cabin. This metaphorical cabin that we've been simulating, now we can actually do it without also having to be off-rid in the sense of it. we really aren't around any civilization.

>> It actually became a lucky accident given the real estate crunch that is happening all over America and certainly in in Boone. Uh we had to be beggars more than choosers in the place where we live. There just wasn't a lot available on the market. Um and so we were able to rent something just by accident that happened to be between the mountains that didn't get sales service. So it wasn't on purpose at all. And in fact, we installed the internet when we first moved in. We're just living a normal life. We have a baby coming. We have to have the internet. what if something happens? We didn't even even think that um it would be possible to do it until

we found out what living with full-time Wi-Fi did to us. We had to re understand this or I would I use us, but it's really certainly me I think is is the real problem in this. Um we live about 12 to 15 minutes from town. Um I can get a celli signal a mile away if I want to get closer and just send an email off or something like that. But really um once we turned off the internet, it required me to drive into town to my office or to a library or coffee shop. And and that really allows me to um segregate work

life from home life. I go to work, I do my work, it turns off, I come home and I spend time with my son and my family. Um and and that separation I think is really really [clears throat] essential, Cal. um we have blended these things out of convenience and for some people look it's been it's been really great but I think there is a cost to to that choice um there's a bargain we've made that um your boss can always reach you um and that you can always be distracted always wonder is there an email um whereas what I really try to do is I close the laptop

and that's my time away from the office and now I'm I'm home and that separation um has has made things a lot better um for us and I would recommend that people in their own try to find a way to kind of draw a strong line between work and home life if they can. >> Well, I have some I have some questions about this because I'm interested. So, like let's start with work. Um people are used to So, you have bosses, right? I mean, you have bosses, department chairs, I assume, at the university. Um when you're working on uh articles, freelance, you have editors. Did people just adjust? Like tell me

about people fear if I'm not available like if I don't I'm not around to answer that email at 5 because I'm home and I won't be around till the next morning it's going to be a big problem. It's going to everything is going to fall apart. What was the reality of the lack of communication at home when it when it came to your work? What what what ended up happening with the other people in your professional life? >> Far less than I ever anticipated. I actually I think you say this all the time on your show. We will um for sure have a mailman on a horse deliver a photograph of this interview once once this is the downside of doing what you did is you're going you're going to get a lot of bad like jokes and aides and reactionary critiques. So that that's probably just the trade-off you're you're willing to make is a lot of telegraph jokes I assume. But that's probably a fair trade. But I appreciate you coming on the show. >> Thank you so much Cal. It's been great to be here.

Cal’s closing remarks

>> All right. So there you have it. That was my conversation with Chris Moody. Uh, I thought it was fascinating. I think what he's up to out there in Boone has some lessons for all of us. And remember to check out the the new Substack, the opt outers that Chris started with his wife if you want to keep up with what they're up to and the lessons they have for the rest of us. I got to tell you though, here's something that's kind of interesting. Chris and I, it turns out, have all of these uh these sort of unexpected connections that we keep discovering. All right, let me give you some

examples. I recorded this interview right before leaving for a trip out to Colorado. I was going to a small town in Colorado with my uh family for vacation. And when I called up Chris to do this interview before I left for the trip, I was like, "Oh, where are you recording from?" Because I know he doesn't have internet in his cabin. He was staying with family uh a family they know in the same small town I was about to go out to and visit. All right. Right. Unexpected connection. Unexpected connection number two. Chris's grandfather was a Southern

Baptist minister who knew well my grandfather who was alo also a Southern Baptist minister. I think um my grandfather had maybe taught uh or mentored his grandfather. Also, it turns out that the town Boon where Chris lives, I believe, named for Daniel Boone. And I am a descendant, I can't really say, of Daniel Boone. I'm descended from Daniel Boone's brother. My my my grandmother's uh middle name um was Boon. And so, the connections

too many connections. And of course, the biggest connection of all, we share our distrust of a constantly connected life. So, there we go. fascinating conversation with someone that has a lot of almost like spooky spooky spookily spookily abundant connections to my own life. That's how we know this whole interview was Kismmet. So anyways, I hope you liked it. Um long interview. I'm out of town. So uh we'll skip the normal like Q&A uh and what I'm up to uh that I would normally do, but I'll be back next week with another advice episode. So until then, as always, stay

deep. Hey, if you made it this far, you must be ready to join my fight for depth in a distracted world. item.content:encoded:
YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QPapwLpog0I

Transcript

Do you ever get that sense when you're hearing business executives talk about AI that they seem to be living in a completely different world than the rest of us? I mean, I get that feeling a lot. I want to give you a recent example. Last week, I came across an article from the New York Times business section that interviewed multiple executives from the German software company SAP as well as several European business and economics analysts. Now, what struck me was how confident everyone was that AI had already started massively disrupting

the economy and would continue to do so at an accelerating rate in the near future. Here, let me load the article on the screen here. Look, the title was, "Can you embrace AI without layoffs? This company says it's trying." And look at the subhead here. The German software giant SAP says it's betting that employees can reinvent jobs instead of eliminating them. Experts are divided on whether it will work. All right, so let's think about that wording for a moment. That article, this interview

with the SAP executives takes for granted, right? The people they talk to take for granted that AI, if left unchecked, is poised to eliminate large number of jobs. The only question is whether or not there is something we can come up with to stop that by having maybe new jobs to replace all those that we are for sure about to lose. Now, these are incredibly bold claims and yet they're made so confidently and so casually when you hear business executives talk. And to me, this raises some key questions such as why is the business community so confident that AI

will definitely eliminate lots of existing jobs? What is it that executives and SAP are seeing about their own employees and their clients that makes them think that these massive changes are imminent? And most importantly, are they right? Well, it's Thursday, which means it's time for an AI reality check episode of this podcast, which is the perfect opportunity to go seeking some measured answers. All right, so here's my plan. I'm going to dive deeper into this article and try to better understand what the business community over there in Europe actually believes about AI. and then I'll step back and give you my

take. I want to give a trigger warning here. If you're an executive at one of these companies or a business analyst, uh you might not like the conclusions I end up reaching. All right, anyways, let's dive in. As always, I'm Kell Newport and this is Deep Questions, the show for people seeking depth in a distracted world. [music] All right. So, I want to return to the article here uh and read another quote from it that I I think sets the stage for how executives at SAP are thinking

about AI and its impact. So, I'll put this on the screen here and read it. Its leaders concede that AI is eliminating the need for humans to do many of the tasks it software engineers did until very recently. In a round of restructuring two years ago, SAP cut nearly 10,000 jobs, some as a result of AI, the company said. All right, I want to stop right there. That's an incredible claim. So, the executive cited in this article, it said that the job cuts they did two years ago were in part in response to AI.

So, in the spring of 2024, they claimed they were laying people off because of the power of AI. Well, look, I've been reporting and writing about AI since the beginning of ChatGpt. Let me bring you back to the spring of 2024. The state-of-the-art generative AI in the spring of 2024 was Chat GPT powered by GPT40, which its main claim to fame is that there was more input types it could accept than GPT4. you could have uh like for example audio as input. So it was like a multimodal thing. There were no

real programming harnesses back then. The very first uh serious programming harness, Devon, had just been released that spring in a highly restricted experimental form. So there's no one using AI in any systematic way to program. We were still mainly talking about the potential for this this technology in the future. We were still dealing with relatively limited chat bots. So this sort of this claim, uh, yeah, those layoffs we did were also part of AI, I mean, it feels like that's just essentially made up. Now, we have other

sources we can turn to here. Um, as I covered in an AI reality check episode of this show back in May, in the last few months, many technology leaders have come out to say really clearly that that narrative that people were uh, laying people off because of AI just hasn't been accurate. Let me remind you of some of these quotes. Nvidia CEO Jensen Wong said, "Claims that AI would eliminate large number of jobs were quote ridiculous." He also said the following, and I'm quoting him here, "It was just a way for executives to sound smart, and I

really hate that. I think they're scaring people, and that's irresponsible." Venture capitalist Mark Andre also has this spring ridiculed the idea that AI could be responsible for software development job losses already given the fact that mature AI coding tools were only just became available this fall. He notes that cuts in development jobs like the cuts that SAP made two years ago or more a combination of factors such as correcting for overhiring of tech companies during COVID and increase in interest rate which requires them to actually uh reduce expenditures to keep

profit numbers where they need to be. The most recent data backs this up. There's a new report out that reveals that tech job openings rebounded sharply in 2026. The number of software development job openings at the moment is at its highest level in three years. Even Sam Alman in a conference last May said his fears of mass job losses had turned out to be wrong. Let me read his quote here. I'm delighted to be wrong about this. I thought there would have been more impact on entry-level white collar jobs being eliminated by now than has actually happened. All right, so

let's step back. I think because I think this is really critical. Basically, every major figure close to the current AI boon has said this idea that layoffs were happening in the past couple of years due to AI is just wrong. They also are largely eliminating the idea that we are going to face massive job losses due to AI in the near future. And yet the executives from SAP quoted in this article casually just threw out, oh yeah, we uh in the restructuring we

did a couple years ago like some of that was AI. We had to replace people because of AI. So they were presenting that claim as if that was obviously true, even though a closer look at the reality shows that nothing like that is true. All right, let's read further in the article to get some more insight into the way these business executives think about AI. I'm going to bring another quote up here on the screen. I'm I'm reading now from the article. I'm not sure uh I'm not sure if here someone in two or three years will still code software. Christian Klein, the chief executive, told me in a recent interview. He said he did not expect to

operate with a smaller workforce, but with a very, very different workforce. Such a strategy could be a source of hope for Europe. Economists say it might prevent large-scale job losses in some sectors while plugging unfilled vacancies in others. Europe, an aging continent, uh, is facing a long fate of slow economic growth, has a chronic lack of skilled workers. All right, I want to break down that passage from the article because there's some uh there's some key leaps of logic in here that I really want to emphasize. All right, so it starts by the chief executive of SAP noting that AI tools are now much more

involved in the actual production of computer code. This is true. programmers uh now as of 2026, this sort of this last quarter, now nearly ubiquitously work closely with AI agents. They in interactive conversations with the agents, specify exactly what piece of code they want. The agent produces and tests the code. The humans look at it and then go back and forth if it's not quite what they want. So, the actual typing of computer code has been uh greatly reduced. There's more and more of the actual typing of code that's coming out of a model that's working interactively with computer programmers.

Okay, but as we just noted with all those quotes we read before, this has not led to software jobs disappearing. There's now a record high number of job listings in software development. We're still trying to understand exactly the best way to work with these agents, but it is certainly not replacing programmers. Maybe it will, but it's not right now, and it's just as likely that it won't. But that reality doesn't show up in this quote because if we go further, the chief executive of SAP goes on to imply that if AI's coding capabilities are not addressed, those software development uh

jobs will disappear. Right? Because remember he said, and I'll bring this back up here. Um he did not expect to operate with a smaller workforce, but with a very very different workforce. Right? The implication there is that they would be operating with a much smaller workforce because these jobs are going to go away. But he will avoid that fate for his programmers by finding them different types of work to do what he's calling a very very different workforce. They get into it later in the article that you know it's going to be more about being a forward deployed engineer and and orchestrating AI or something like this

right so his implication is if we don't invent new jobs we're going to lose all these software development jobs. Then comes the even bigger leap of logic. The the quote goes on to say that actually there will be and I'll put this on the screen largecale job losses in other sectors of Europe due to AI like that's the default assumption that's what's going to happen if we don't do anything else but if the rest of the economy that there's some silver linings here is that um actually if we plug in

the SAP strategy of inventing new AIA work for these workers that all those jobs won't disappear. And then it goes on to say, and also the fact that a lot of these jobs, of course, are going to be automated is maybe not that bad of a thing because we're we have a labor crunch coming as we age out workers. There's not going to be enough skilled workers to fill the current jobs. So maybe it's not a bad thing that a lot of those are going to be automated. So at the core of this sort of logic here from the chief executive is this idea that software jobs, if nothing else changes, will go away. that at SAP they will find other work for those uh programmers new types of jobs that

involve coordinating AI and in other sectors unrelated to computer programming they're also going to lose a lot of jobs but some of those they'll be able to redirect in other places and in other cases automating jobs will be okay because we don't have enough workers anyways so again there is just this casual confident assumption that AI is in the process of eliminating lots of jobs or soon will eliminate lots of jobs not just in computer programming but in multiple sectors across the European an economy. All right. Well, you might be wondering maybe like what's really going on here is that internally at SAP they have

found really innovative ways to use AI and that's why they're so sure that all these other sectors are about to be eliminated. Well, fortunately we can get some insight because in this article the SAP executives go on to summarize how they are currently using AI within their company. We're about to see here some like truly [snorts] I'm I'm assuming very impressive, super powerful automation. So, let's read what they said here. SAP workers use AI tools to try to improve applications for patents and to handle some customer support request. Its AI agents code

prototypes for new software or add new features to existing programs, speeding up the process for developing products. Okay. So, within SAP, the way they're using AI is to uh generate or clean up some writing on applications to do some in quotation marks, customer support tickets. Um, the Vibe Code prototypes and the developers are using agents to help them when they're adding new features. Uh, I mean, I guess us humans are

obsolete now. I mean, I'm being sarcastic, of course, because these are these same narrow use cases we've heard for a long time. The only interesting one is programmers are now ubiquitously using these tools. We don't know what that means, but they're ubiquously using those tools. But this idea of it can help you write drafts of things or clean up text or maybe it can be like a chatbot for some customer service. We've been saying that for years. It hasn't done anything to the economy. And so if that is what is happening within SAP with AI, how do they get from that to multiple sectors of the economy

are going to lose huge numbers of jobs because of this technology, but that's okay because we have a labor shortage anyways and we have enough people to fill those jobs anyways. How do you jump from these? There's nothing new here. This is the same narrow use cases we've been hearing about for a long time. And yet they've jumped from that to this confidence of like yeah software development jobs are going away but we can find new jobs for them and other sectors will lose a lot of jobs too but you know what it might not be so bad because we don't have enough people to fill those jobs and younger people we can invent new jobs that are like orchestrating AI so maybe it'll be okay and the headline of the whole piece is

like yeah but the experts they interviewed are like maybe but maybe that won't work at all like it's a 50-50 chance about whether we're basically about to go through a massive economic depression or maybe we can kind of muddle our way through it. There is such confidence here that economic devastation is coming even though we just looked at the last three months of the technology press is all these leaders saying like that's overblown that's executives trying to sound smart. We don't really expect there to be massive job losses. There is a huge disconnect here between the casual confidence of the business community as exemplified by the quotes in this article and reality.

Well, what explains this? What explains what's going on here, right? We don't have how 9000 right now. We're not in azimoff iroot short story. We have a cool new programming utility that we're still trying to figure out and some like truly mediocre narrow business applications. That's the reality. How do we get from there to this casual confidence that the economy is going to be destroyed if not for like some like very uh creative reinvention and pivoting by business leaders? Well, here's my emerging theory. Many business executives and analysts

don't really understand AI much at all. They are operating on vague vibes or reacting to things that they've sort of heard endlessly repeated on LinkedIn that seem directionally true. I also think that a lot of people in these situations are more afraid of missing a disruption than they are about being wrong about a disruption that doesn't happen. There's just more credibility and feel feeling like you're very AI forward to say, oh yeah, we laid off people uh was an interest rates as AI. It makes you sound like you're AI

forward to be like, I bravely know as some seuite executive at a massive software company, I bravely recognize that the economy is about the crater, but we're going to pivot and be smart about it. Makes you seem AI forward. It makes you seem high-tech. But I keep hearing this again and again from individuals who are talking to their managers like I don't think they understand what AI is at all. They're they're they're repeating like slop from LinkedIn that makes no sense. You better be using AI or someone who uses AI will replace you. And like to do what though? What part of my job is AI going to make better? What

do you want me to? And they're just like AI good job go away. Mec person on Lincoln say that all software dev go away. Me not want that. I I guess the managers talk like um caveman. Is that how that works? But I think this is putting us in a difficult situation, right? Think about it as the as the just the American public or the world public here. On the one hand, we have the people who arguably know most about the technology, which are the AI executives that have this weird addiction to doom trolling. So, we have a hard time listening to them and they're kind of going back and forth. They seem to be a

little bit better recently, maybe because of pending IPOs. They're a little better recently about like, yeah, we're okay. It's not going to take jobs. But then every once, but the AI is going to take over, kill us all, and then they go back. So, they have this weird addiction to doom trolling. So it's hard to sort of pay too much attention to the AI executives. But now we have the people who are most impacted by the technology, the people who run companies who uh are dealing almost exclusively in vibes and sort of like things that they heard on LinkedIn that sound directionally true. They seem completely disconnected from the reality of what's really happening with AI.

So how are we supposed to understand what's really going on? We can't trust the people who know the most about it. We can't trust the people most impacted by it. Of course, we're all confused about it. I think one of the solutions here is journalism. Um, I think journalists, here's my idea. I think journalists, they need to change their frame when they think about AI. And it can, they cannot approach it like you would approach like normal technology reporting or business reporting. I think we have to bring a frame of skepticism and criticality to AI reporting that's similar to what we do for political reporting. It's very important what happens in this sector. A lot of impacts

are going to happen, but we don't just trust or take for granted or accept whatever the people we interview happen to say because they all have their own agendas or biases or blind spots. So and so says this, someone else says this, this claim was made by this CEO. Uh these other people completely dispute that claim. We talked to East Coast computer scientists who don't wear robes and go to X-Risk cult sacrifice meetings about what this technology actually means. And here's what they said. We have to bring the same skepticism you bring to like a presidential or the congressional midterms that are

happening now. It's incredibly important. The impacts are big and we don't trust the word out of almost anyone's mouth. And that'll change the way I think the public understands AI as well. We'll be less susceptible to this doom thing we saw over here, this confident prediction here. The skeptic that dismisses everything over there. if we we put on our political reporting blinders or glasses or whatever we want to call it, I think we'll be able to navigate this important moment better. Now, obviously, I want to give a caveat here. Many, many business leaders and managers know a lot about AI and they're very savvy about it and

they're very clearheaded about it. I've talked to a lot of these managers, but there is a class of people right now in the business community who are very vocal who really have no idea what they're talking about and they're causing a lot of confusion for people who read their quotes and they're causing a lot of pain for the people who work under them who are like, I don't know what you're saying. This is like a Dilbert column cartoon from hell. All right, so that's my plea. be wary, just as wary about what business leaders are confidently and casually saying about AI as you are about the doom that's coming out of the mouth of AI tech CEOs. All right, that's

it for this week. Um, I probably will I may or may not have another AI reality check episode next week. I'm traveling again. Summer I travel a lot, so we'll see if I can get one in. But otherwise, I'll be back the week after. And on Monday though, there will be an advice episode of the show. So definitely tune in for that as well. Uh, and until next time, remember, care about AI, but not necessarily everything you read about it. Hey, if you made it this far, you must be ready to join my fight for depth in a distracted world. Now, the best way to do this is to join over 125,000 people who receive my email newsletter

each Monday. You can sign up at calupport.com/idas. [music] And when you do, I will send you a free guide to my seven best ideas about cultivating a deep life. Sign up today, calber.com/idas.

Tell me if this sounds familiar: you buy a beautiful notebook, excited by all its possibilities to help refine your thoughts and generate new insights. Then it sits unused until you forget about it.
